beforeTrip.pageTitle: Before you go | Korea Travel Guide
beforeTrip.title: Before you go
beforeTrip.intro: A guide to what to prepare and double-check before you leave for your trip. For tips during travel, see the Travel Tips category.
beforeTrip.docs1: Confirm passport validity (6+ months beyond return) and whether you need a visa or K-ETA.
beforeTrip.docs2: Keep hotel address, purpose of stay, and return ticket ready. File e-Arrival (ERI) in its own tab.
beforeTrip.docs3: Travel insurance helps with medical costs, lost items, and delays.
beforeTrip.money1: Cards are common, but markets and some shops need cash — carry about ₩50,000–100,000.
beforeTrip.money2: Compare airport/city exchange and ATMs; check foreign-transaction fees.
beforeTrip.money3: Buy a T-money-style transit card on day one. See the Wow Pass tab for the tourist prepaid option.
beforeTrip.connect1: Get an eSIM or SIM for data — free Wi-Fi alone is unreliable for maps.
beforeTrip.connect2: Install and sign into maps (Naver/Kakao), translation (Papago), and messaging before you fly.
beforeTrip.connect3: Note your eSIM install and activation steps so maps work on landing.
beforeTrip.power1: Korea uses 220V and Type C/F plugs (round pins). Hotels use the same.
beforeTrip.power2: Type A (flat-pin) devices need a travel adapter. Most chargers are 100–240V, so an adapter alone is enough.
beforeTrip.power3: A power bank and multi-port charger make all-day apps easier.
beforeTrip.pack1: Seoul involves lots of walking — pack seasonal clothes and comfortable shoes.
beforeTrip.pack2: Book early for peak seasons; note check-in and luggage storage.
beforeTrip.pack3: Bring familiar meds, toiletries, and spare masks.
beforeTrip.pack4: Leave suitcase space for Olive Young, Daiso, and snack gifts — they add up fast.
beforeTrip.taxi1: As of 2026, Seoul medium (regular) taxis start at ₩4,800 for the first 1.6 km, then distance and time fares apply.
beforeTrip.taxi2: Late night (10 PM–4 AM) adds about 20% or 40% by hour. Other cities may price differently.
beforeTrip.taxi3: Hail on the street or call Kakao T. Cards are common; tipping is not expected.
beforeTrip.taxi4: Naver/Kakao Map car directions often show a rough taxi fare. Overcharging is rare today; apps are a calm optional choice.
beforeTrip.solo1:
Why solo dining can feel hard

Korea’s food culture often assumes sharing. Two-person minimums (samgyeopsal, dakgalbi), big table spreads, and social norms can make walking in alone feel awkward.
beforeTrip.solo2:
If you must go alone

Choose 1-person-friendly spots: kimbap, snack bars, simple set meals, stay-cafés, fast-casual, convenience-store food. A short “just one” usually gets you seated. Kiosks/mobile order help too.
beforeTrip.solo3:
Meet a friend if you can

Dining with a local friend, classmate, or language-exchange partner is easier and opens more restaurants. Book a meetup before your trip to skip solo-dining stress.
beforeTrip.immigration1: SES (Smart Entry Service) is automated immigration via dedicated gates using your passport and biometrics. When eligible, it is often faster than staffed counters.
beforeTrip.immigration2: Used by registered foreigners, some nationalities, and pre-enrolled travelers. Enrollment may add a stamp or SES sticker to your passport. Confirm eligibility on official Immigration / Hi Korea pages.
beforeTrip.immigration3: At the airport, follow SES / automated immigration signs. If you are not eligible, use the regular foreigner counters.
beforeTrip.catEntryIntro: Documents, e-Arrival (ERI), and airport immigration — what to check before you land.
beforeTrip.catMoneyIntro: Cash, cards, transit cards, and the tourist Wow Pass.
beforeTrip.catLifeIntro: Data and power, packing and lodging, transit and taxis, plus a few basic greetings for day-one comfort.
beforeTrip.catDiningIntro: Dining culture and solo meals — helpful to know before you arrive.
beforeTrip.eri1: The e-Arrival Card is Korea’s online arrival declaration (often called ERI). It is separate from K-ETA and the old COVID Q-CODE.
beforeTrip.eri2: File from 3 days before arrival (KST). Validity expires 72 hours after submission. The official portal is free.
beforeTrip.eri3: Submit at https://www.e-arrivalcard.go.kr with passport and stay details. An issue number is emailed to you.
beforeTrip.wowpass1: Wow Pass is a tourist prepaid card often used for shopping and T-money-style transit.
beforeTrip.wowpass2: Issue and top up at airport/station/hotel kiosks; check balances in the app. Shopping and transit wallets are often separate.
beforeTrip.wowpass3: If you already have a no-FX-fee card, a simple T-money card may be enough — choose based on your needs.
beforeTrip.catScheduleIntro: Public holidays and tougher travel periods — handy when picking dates.
beforeTrip.holidays1: Fixed solar dates: New Year (1/1), Independence Movement Day (3/1), Children’s Day (5/5), Memorial Day (6/6), Liberation Day (8/15), National Foundation Day (10/3), Hangul Day (10/9), Christmas (12/25).
beforeTrip.holidays2: Seollal, Chuseok, and Buddha’s Birthday follow the lunar calendar and move each year — typically Seollal in Jan–Feb, Chuseok in Sep–Oct, Buddha’s Birthday in Apr–May. Check that year’s calendar before you fly.
beforeTrip.holidays3: During long weekends, transport and lodging get busy and some shops close. Book early, as in peak season.
beforeTrip.avoid1: Midsummer (Jul–Aug) is hot and humid — outdoor-heavy trips can be tough for first-timers.
beforeTrip.avoid2: The jangma monsoon is roughly late June–July with frequent rain. Indoor plans and flexible schedules help.
beforeTrip.avoid3: Midwinter (Dec–Feb) is cold and windy, especially inland. Not a “don’t come” — just expect more prep if you’re new or plan lots outdoors.
beforeTrip.transit1: In Seoul, subway and bus are often easier and more predictable than renting or driving — less traffic and parking stress.
beforeTrip.transit2: Use Naver/Kakao Map transit routes for transfers and exits. With heavy bags or late at night, also see the Taxi tab.
beforeTrip.transit3: Buying/topping up T-money, Cashbee, or Climate Card is under Money and Wow Pass. Bus tap-out tips are in Travel tips.
beforeTrip.transit4: Some regions (and Jeju) suit rental cars. Even using transit just in Seoul makes day one calmer.
beforeTrip.culture1: Spoon for rice and soup, chopsticks for banchan and meat feels natural. Avoid standing chopsticks upright in rice.
beforeTrip.culture2: Banchan is shared; order together when you’re in a group. Ask for milder spice if you need it.
beforeTrip.culture3: Use a call bell or a small “저기요.” Water/banchan are often self-serve. Pay at the counter; tipping isn’t expected.
beforeTrip.culture4: Looking around once helps more than perfect etiquette.
beforeTrip.korean1: Before you fly, learn a few greetings, thanks, and simple lines. Start with short phrases like “안녕하세요,” “감사합니다,” and “죄송합니다” — not long sentences.
beforeTrip.korean2: Koreans understand that visitors may not speak Korean. Still, asking politely and kindly often brings a warmer response.
beforeTrip.korean3: For ready-to-use lines in restaurants, transit, and shopping, see Useful Korean. A quick look before departure helps a lot.

tips.dailyCardDesc: Maps, trash, weekend rates, convenience stores, rainy days
tips.mapMistake: Using only Google Maps while navigating
tips.mapBody: For transit, walking, and shops on the ground, Naver Map and Kakao Map are often more accurate. Keep Google Maps if you like, but prefer Korean map apps for transfers and exit numbers.
tips.cardMistake: Not tapping when you get off the bus
tips.cardBody: On buses you usually need to tap again when you exit for the fare/transfer to calculate correctly. Buy and top up cards under Before You Go → Money. Follow map-app routes for transfers.
tips.restaurantMistake: Assuming restaurants work the same as abroad
tips.restaurantBody1: You might wait for staff to take your order when there is a call bell at the table, or ask for water and side dishes when there is a self-service station. More places now use kiosks or tablets for ordering, which can be another hurdle if you do not read Korean.
tips.restaurantBody2: Tipping is not common at typical Korean restaurants — you usually do not leave cash or add tip on a card.
tips.restaurantBody3: Abroad, staff often bring the bill to your table. In many Korean restaurants, you finish eating and then pay at the counter near the entrance.
tips.cashBody: Most places take cards, but traditional markets, street stalls, and some small restaurants/taxis are cash-only. Keep small bills.
tips.trashBody: Public bins are fewer than many visitors expect. Use convenience stores, stations, or cafés — or take small trash back to your hotel.
tips.wifiBody: Public Wi-Fi can be unstable. An eSIM/SIM keeps maps, translation, and payment apps online.
tips.queueMistake: Sitting down without checking the queue
tips.queueBody: Popular restaurants often use waiting apps or number tickets at the door. If staff say “one moment,” check the line first.
tips.waterMistake: Waiting for staff to bring everything
tips.waterBody: Many places have a self-serve station for water, utensils, and banchan. Look around once you sit.
tips.rushBody: Weekdays 7–9 a.m. and 6–8 p.m. are packed. Avoid those times if you can, or take a taxi with heavy bags.
tips.taxiMistake: Only explaining the address out loud
tips.taxiBody: Use Kakao T / Uber-style apps, or show the destination in Korean. Ask for a receipt if you need one.
tips.exitBody: Exit numbers matter a lot. Check the recommended exit in your map app before you leave the station.
tips.weekendMistake: Assuming a mid-trip weekend stay costs the same as a weekday
tips.weekendBody: Friday–Sunday and holidays often jump in price for same-day or extended stays. When you change plans, compare dates again in booking apps. For packing/booking before departure, see Before You Go → Packing.
tips.noTipMistake: Korea generally does not tip at restaurants
tips.noTipBody: Typical Korean restaurants and cafés have no tipping culture — service is treated as included. Default: no tip.
tips.catDailyIntro: Maps, trash, weekend rates, convenience stores, and rainy days — everyday tips while you’re traveling.
tips.catRestaurantIntro: Ordering, tipping, waiting lines, and self-serve corners — tips at the table.
tips.catTransportIntro: Tap-out, rush hour, exits, and light etiquette for moving around. Fares and card setup are in Before You Go.
tips.catShoppingIntro: Olive Young, Daiso, duty-free, and markets — all inline here (no extra page hops).
tips.convenienceMistake: Thinking convenience stores are only for snacks
tips.convenienceBody: CU, GS25, and 7-Eleven are everywhere. Grab simple meals and drinks, umbrellas and toiletries, and light quasi-drug items (patches, bandages, etc. — for stronger medicine, ask a pharmacy). Some stores have power-bank rental or charging corners. For combo ideas, see the site’s convenience-store guide.
tips.rainMistake: Heading out without a plan when it suddenly rains
tips.rainBody: If rain starts, buy an umbrella at a convenience store or Daiso. Shift to cafés, museums, or underground malls — or take a short taxi hop. Station connecting passages help you stay dry.
tips.etiquetteMistake: Blocking the doors or taking loud phone calls
tips.etiquetteBody: Let exiting riders leave first, and offer priority seats when someone needs them. Use earphones and keep voices low for calls/videos. Wear your backpack in front or set it down in crowds.

emergency.title: Emergency Information
emergency.desc: For life-threatening emergencies call 112 (police) or 119 (fire/ambulance). Use 1330 for tourist help, 1345 for immigration (weekdays), 1339 for non-emergency medical guidance, and 1588-5644 (BBB) for volunteer phone interpretation.
emergency.embassyNote: For a lost passport or consular emergencies, contact your own embassy or consulate first. Numbers differ by nationality — save the official contact before you fly.
emergency.passportNote: If you lose your passport, file a report with police (112) and ask your embassy about an emergency travel document. Call 1330 if you need tourist interpretation help.

apps.kakaoDesc: Strong for directions, transit, and taxis. Shop info is usually accurate because locals use it heavily.
apps.naverDesc: Detailed subway/bus transfers and live arrivals. Great walking routes too.
apps.papagoDesc: Korean↔English/Japanese translation plus photo text recognition — perfect for menus.
apps.talkDesc: Korea’s main messenger. Needed for hotels, tours, and adding local contacts.
apps.yanoljaDesc: Hotels, motels, and guesthouses with frequent same-day deals.
apps.yeogiDesc: Easy stay comparison and reviews. Photos and maps help even if the UI is Korean.
apps.coupangDesc: Groceries and food delivery. Often accepts foreign cards — handy for short stays.
apps.baeminDesc: Korea’s most popular food delivery app. The UI is Korean, but photos and maps make ordering easy — great for hotel delivery on short trips.
apps.yogiyoDesc: Another major delivery app alongside Baemin. Shops and coupons differ — worth comparing both.
apps.tmoneyDesc: Check transit card balance/top-up and some mobility services in one app.
apps.kakaoTDesc: Taxis, designated drivers, bikes, and parking in one app. Foreign cards are often accepted.

shopping.intro: From Olive Young and Daiso to duty-free and markets — shopping tips visitors ask about most.
shopping.olive1: Start with ‘Olive Young Picks’ and sale shelves. Sheet masks, sunscreen, and tints are popular gifts.
shopping.olive2: App/membership coupons can add discounts — ask staff about similar items on sale.
shopping.olive3: Airport/Myeongdong stores stock tourist sets; neighborhood stores may differ in stock and price.
shopping.daiso1: Great for fixed-price household goods, stationery, and travel bits that fit a suitcase.
shopping.daiso2: Floors are categorized — follow in-store signs for travel/storage keywords.
shopping.duty1: Downtown/airport duty-free may need passport and flight info — check pickup rules.
shopping.duty2: Shop tax-free needs a minimum spend, passport, and airport refund steps. Look for TAX FREE signs.
shopping.market1: Gwangjang, Namdaemun, and Dongdaemun sometimes prefer cash — ask if cards work.
shopping.market2: Myeongdong, Hongdae, and Gangnam mix brands and street food; weekends get crowded.

fun.pcbangDesc: 24-hour PC cafés with fast machines and internet — great for gaming or catching up on work.
fun.noraebangDesc: Pay-per-song coin noraebang — easy solo or with friends.
fun.escapeDesc: Solve puzzles against the clock. Many shops in Hongdae and Gangnam.
fun.jjimDesc: Korean bathhouse culture — saunas, heated floors, and overnight lounging.
fun.pcbangBody1: A PC bang (PC cafe) rents high-spec computers by the hour. Travelers use them for online games, video calls, paperwork, and charging devices. 24-hour shops are common near nightlife, campuses, and stations.
fun.pcbangBody2: Staff or a kiosk assigns a seat; you prepay with cash, card, or QR. Extend time at the counter when the on-screen timer runs low. Many shops let you order drinks, ramyeon, or snacks from the desk or an in-seat menu.
fun.pcbangPrice:
Price vibe

Roughly ₩1,000–₩2,000 per hour (late night or premium seats cost more). Food and drinks are extra.
fun.pcbangTip:
Tips

ID is rarely required. Keep quiet for neighbors, log out of accounts, and clear USB files. Some shops have separate smoking areas — follow the signs.
fun.noraebangBody1: Coin karaoke is pay-per-song (or short time) self-karaoke — easier solo/small groups than hourly private rooms. Common in Hongdae, Gangnam, campuses, and near stations.
fun.noraebangBody2: Insert cash or top up by card/QR, then search songs — English/Japanese catalogs are common. Watch remaining songs/time.
fun.noraebangPrice:
Price vibe

About ₩500–₩1,000 per song, or short time packs — varies by shop and hour.
fun.noraebangTip:
Tips

Weekend nights can mean waits. Keep volume considerate and treat mics/gear gently.
fun.escapeBody1: Escape rooms put your team in a themed room to solve puzzles within about 60 minutes. Clusters sit in Hongdae, Gangnam, Konkuk, and Daehangno; more venues offer English hints.
fun.escapeBody2: Book a theme, time, and party size online. Staff brief you on rules and the panic button. Check difficulty stars and genre (horror, mystery, cozy) first. Hints usually come via walkie-talkie or screen.
fun.escapePrice:
Price vibe

Often about ₩20,000–₩30,000 per person. Some themes charge more for pairs — check the booking page.
fun.escapeTip:
Tips

Arrive on time. Never force or break props. Read warnings on horror rooms. Follow photo and spoiler policies.
fun.jjimBody1: A jjimjilbang is a Korean spa complex with baths, saunas, heated-floor lounges, and nap zones — popular for overnight rests or recovering from jet lag.
fun.jjimBody2: Lock shoes and valuables, get a wristband, shower in the gendered bath area, then wear the provided clothes in shared lounges. Large chains with English signs are easier for first-timers.
fun.jjimPrice:
Price vibe

Entry often ₩10,000–₩20,000, with late-night or weekend surcharges. Food, towels, and robes may cost extra.
fun.jjimTip:
Tips

Always shower before soaking. Keep quiet, lock valuables, and watch your bags in sleep rooms. Tattoo and swimsuit rules vary — read the front desk signs.
fun.lotteDesc: Indoor/outdoor theme park in Jamsil — easy subway day trip.
fun.lotteBody1: Lotte World is a combined indoor/outdoor park in central Jamsil. You can ride even on rainy days, and Lotte World Tower plus Seokchon Lake are nearby for a full day plan.
fun.lotteBody2: Buy tickets online or at kiosks, then explore Adventure (indoor) and Magic Island (outdoor). Weekends get crowded — hit popular rides early.
fun.lottePrice:
Price vibe

Day tickets vary by season and promos. Check the official site/app first.
fun.lotteTip:
Tips

Linked to Lines 2 & 8 Jamsil Station. Use lockers for big bags; evening parades and night views are worth planning for.
fun.everlandDesc: Yongin’s flagship theme park — a full-day outing for families and friends.
fun.everlandBody1: Everland is Korea’s classic large theme park in Yongin, Gyeonggi — coasters, safari areas, and seasonal festivals that easily fill a day.
fun.everlandBody2: Reach it via Everline, shuttle, or bus from Bundang Line stations like Jukjeon/Giheung. Ride popular attractions at opening, and plan indoor/shade routes on hot or rainy days.
fun.everlandPrice:
Price vibe

Online advance tickets are often better than walk-up prices. Safari or special experiences may cost extra.
fun.everlandTip:
Tips

Wear comfortable shoes. Peak days mean longer waits — check live transit in a map app.
fun.mangaDesc: Time-based café where you browse manga with drinks and light snacks.
fun.mangaBody1: Manga cafés rent seats by the hour so you can read Korean/Japanese comics and magazines. Common near Hongdae, Sinchon, and campuses — great for quiet solo time.
fun.mangaBody2: Pay for time (and often a drink) at the desk, then pick a seat. New releases may be limited — reshelve books when done.
fun.mangaPrice:
Price vibe

Often a few thousand won per hour plus a drink; some offer late-night/day passes.
fun.mangaTip:
Tips

Follow food/drink rules; keep quiet and ask before photos. Settle at the counter before leaving.
fun.boardgameDesc: Cafés with huge board-game libraries for friends and families.
fun.boardgameBody1: Pay a cover/time fee, borrow games, and order drinks. Many shops teach rules — beginner-friendly even without Korean.
fun.boardgameBody2: Tell staff your group size and tastes for recommendations. Weekends often need bookings; borrow 1–2 games at a time.
fun.boardgamePrice:
Price vibe

Often a few thousand to ~₩10,000 per person/hour plus a drink order.
fun.boardgameTip:
Tips

Watch for missing pieces; ask if English rulebooks are available.
fun.unmannedDesc: Staff-light convenience and snack shops with kiosk/camera checkout.
fun.unmannedBody1: Unmanned shops let you enter and pay without a cashier — convenience, snack, or variety formats near campuses and stations.
fun.unmannedBody2: Entry may need QR, PIN, or card auth. Scan barcodes at the kiosk and pay by card/pay-app. CCTV is normal — shop politely.
fun.unmannedPrice:
Price vibe

Similar to convenience stores (sometimes a bit cheaper). Some stay open late.
fun.unmannedTip:
Tips

Have a backup if foreign cards fail. Read the door sticker for entry steps when locked.
fun.photoboothDesc: Life4Cut / Photoism-style self booths — popular sticker-photo souvenirs.
fun.photoboothBody1: Self photo booths let you pose, pick frames, and print on the spot — a Korea trip staple in Hongdae, Myeongdong, Seongsu, Gangnam.
fun.photoboothBody2: Pick people/prints/frames on the kiosk; pay by card, cash, or QR. English UI is common — try another brand if the queue is long.
fun.photoboothPrice:
Price vibe

Often ₩4,000–₩6,000 per set (4 poses). Extra prints/merch vary.
fun.photoboothTip:
Tips

Keep bags tidy, respect session time, and pack prints flat as souvenirs.
fun.choiceFunDesc: PC cafés, karaoke, theme parks, jjimjilbang.

transport.mapAlt: Full-screen interactive map of places in Korea
transport.mapCaption: Tap a pin to see the place intro here
transport.tabsHelp: Tap a tab to view details.
transport.subwayIntro: Each Seoul Metro line has its own color. Station names and transfer signs appear in Korean, English, Japanese, and Chinese. A T-money card is the easiest way to ride buses and the subway.
transport.officialMapDesc: For the most accurate official diagram, open Seoul Metro Cyber Station. Embedding it here is blocked by the site’s policy.
transport.interactiveMapHelp: Choose a line below to highlight it on the map. (Based on real routes — may look different from schematic maps.)
transport.mapSource: Satellite tiles: Esri · Coordinates: guidebook places
transport.linePickHint: Choose a line to highlight it on the map and show a short description below.
transport.subwayTip1: Buy and top up T-money at convenience stores or subway stations.
transport.subwayTip2: Rush hours (weekdays 7–9 a.m., 6–8 p.m.) are very crowded.
transport.subwayTip3: Use Kakao Map or Naver Map for live directions.
